weeks.title: The Financial Crisis, Recovery, and Political Realignment
weeks.essentialQuestion: Why did financial risk become a national crisis, and why did recovery produce continuing political anger?

vocabulary.subprime mortgage: A home loan made to a borrower with higher assessed credit risk.
vocabulary.securitization: Pooling financial assets and selling claims on their cash flows.
vocabulary.systemic risk: Risk that failure in one part of a system can destabilize the whole system.
vocabulary.bailout: Government support intended to prevent collapse of an institution or system.
vocabulary.foreclosure: Legal loss of property after failure to meet mortgage obligations.
vocabulary.Affordable Care Act: A 2010 federal health law expanding coverage and regulating insurance markets.

keyUnderstandings: Housing, leverage, complex securities, weak risk controls, and interconnected finance contributed to the crisis.
Emergency interventions stabilized major institutions but created disputes about fairness, accountability, and moral hazard.
Recovery reduced unemployment over time while wealth loss and regional inequality shaped political reaction.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Rising home prices, expanding mortgage credit, securitization, leverage, and weak underwriting created vulnerability. When housing prices fell and defaults rose, financial institutions could not easily value or absorb losses, credit froze, and the recession deepened.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Federal Reserve action, bank support, fiscal stimulus, auto-industry intervention, and later regulation aimed to prevent collapse and restore demand. Critics disagreed about whether interventions were necessary, insufficient, unfair, or poorly designed.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Students compare a mortgage document, regulator testimony, a homeowner account, financial data, and arguments for and against intervention. They trace mechanisms rather than treating 'Wall Street' or borrowers as a single cause.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: The recovery eventually restored employment and output, but many households lost homes and wealth. The period also saw the election of the first Black president, healthcare reform, Tea Party activism, Occupy Wall Street, and changing party coalitions.

weeks.title: Contemporary America: Institutions, Movements, and Historical Distance
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can students study very recent events responsibly when evidence is abundant, contested, and still developing?

vocabulary.historical distance: The time and perspective available between an event and later interpretation.
vocabulary.misinformation: False or inaccurate information shared without necessarily intending harm.
vocabulary.disinformation: False information deliberately created or spread to deceive.
vocabulary.platform: A digital service that hosts, organizes, or distributes user content.
vocabulary.public health emergency: A serious health event requiring coordinated public action.
vocabulary.peaceful transfer of power: The lawful transition of governing authority after an election.

keyUnderstandings: Recent history requires the same sourcing standards as older history, with added caution about incomplete records.
Digital platforms accelerate participation and information while also amplifying manipulation, fragmentation, and harassment.
Elections, protest movements, the COVID-19 pandemic, and institutional conflict tested public trust and federalism.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: Historians of the recent past work with abundant evidence but limited distance. Official records may be incomplete, legal cases unresolved, and participants still shaping public narratives. Students should therefore distinguish verified event, contemporaneous claim, later finding, and open question.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Social media transformed campaigning, activism, journalism, and community formation. It also enabled rapid misinformation, foreign influence operations, targeted advertising, and algorithmic amplification. Racial-justice protests, gun-policy activism, labor organizing, and other movements used digital tools alongside traditional organizing.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Students compare certified election information, public-health data, court decisions, platform policies, and reporting from outlets with different editorial perspectives. They avoid treating popularity, repetition, or emotional intensity as proof.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: The COVID-19 pandemic tested public-health capacity, federalism, education, employment, and trust. The 2020 election and January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol placed renewed attention on election administration, evidence standards, constitutional procedure, and peaceful transfer of power.

weeks.title: The Constitution in Practice: Federalism and the Courts
weeks.essentialQuestion: How has constitutional meaning changed through amendment, legislation, court decisions, executive action, and civic pressure?

vocabulary.incorporation: Application of Bill of Rights protections to states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
vocabulary.precedent: A prior judicial decision used to guide later cases.
vocabulary.strict scrutiny: A demanding judicial test applied to certain classifications or fundamental rights.
vocabulary.standing: A legal requirement that a party show a sufficient stake in a dispute.
vocabulary.federal preemption: Displacement of state law by valid federal law.
vocabulary.civil liberty: A freedom protected against improper government interference.

keyUnderstandings: Constitutional change occurs through text, amendment, precedent, statute, practice, and political development.
Courts depend on cases, standing, evidence, enforcement, and public institutions rather than acting as abstract councils.
Federalism can protect diversity and experimentation while also creating unequal rights or services across states.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: The Constitution establishes institutions and powers but does not mechanically resolve every modern dispute. Amendments, statutes, executive practices, and court decisions have changed how its principles apply to states, individuals, businesses, and new technology.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Judicial review allows courts to decide constitutional cases, but courts operate within jurisdictional limits and depend on other institutions for implementation. Precedent promotes stability while legal reasoning permits distinction or overruling.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Students compare the reasoning—not merely outcomes—of landmark cases involving speech, criminal procedure, equal protection, privacy, religious liberty, and federalism. They identify facts, constitutional question, holding, rationale, and dissent.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: Florida’s constitution, courts, open-records provisions, local governments, and ballot-amendment process provide a state-level comparison. Civic literacy requires knowing which institution has authority and which remedy is legally available.

weeks.title: Elections, Media, Public Policy, and Civic Participation
weeks.regions: United States, Florida, and local communities
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can citizens influence public policy without sacrificing accuracy, pluralism, or constitutional rights?

vocabulary.primary election: An election used to select party nominees or narrow candidates.
vocabulary.general election: An election in which voters choose among nominees for office.
vocabulary.interest group: An organization seeking to influence public policy.
vocabulary.public opinion: Measured attitudes held by members of a population.
vocabulary.policy analysis: Systematic comparison of a problem, alternatives, evidence, tradeoffs, and implementation.
vocabulary.media literacy: The ability to access, evaluate, create, and act on information responsibly.

keyUnderstandings: Elections are one channel of participation alongside testimony, organizing, litigation, service, journalism, and public comment.
Reliable civic judgment requires source evaluation, quantitative literacy, and recognition of tradeoffs.
Nonpartisan inquiry does not mean avoiding values; it means applying consistent evidence rules across viewpoints.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: American elections operate through federal constitutional rules, state law, local administration, parties, campaigns, and courts. Citizens participate as voters, candidates, volunteers, poll workers, journalists, advocates, donors, and public officials.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Interest groups and social movements aggregate concerns, supply expertise, mobilize members, and pressure institutions. Their influence can widen participation or create unequal access, depending on resources, transparency, and rules.

vocabulary.civic capstone: A culminating investigation applying disciplinary knowledge to a public problem.
vocabulary.stakeholder: A person or group affected by or able to influence a decision.
vocabulary.policy option: A specific course of action available to decision makers.
vocabulary.tradeoff: A benefit sacrificed or cost accepted when choosing among alternatives.
vocabulary.public record: Government information legally available for public inspection, subject to exemptions.
vocabulary.deliberation: Structured discussion that weighs evidence, values, alternatives, and consequences.

keyUnderstandings: Historical knowledge improves civic judgment by revealing origins, constraints, precedents, and unintended consequences.
A strong civic proposal defines authority, stakeholders, evidence, costs, rights, implementation, and evaluation.
Democratic disagreement is productive only when participants follow fair procedures and shared evidence standards.

readingSections.heading: Setting the Stage
readingSections.text: The final week asks students to connect the full course: Indigenous sovereignty, founding principles, slavery and emancipation, industrialization, migration, war, civil rights, economic change, constitutional development, and modern information systems.

readingSections.heading: People, Power, and Systems
readingSections.text: Students choose a nonpartisan local or school-community problem. They identify the responsible institution, research history and current conditions, interview or consult stakeholders, analyze data, compare at least three policy options, and examine constitutional or legal constraints.

readingSections.heading: Reading the Evidence
readingSections.text: Evidence must be traceable. Students maintain a source log, label inference and uncertainty, include a serious counterargument, and correct any unsupported claim. The project may be presented as a policy brief, public exhibit, documentary, hearing simulation, or formal presentation.

readingSections.heading: Why It Matters
readingSections.text: The goal is not ideological agreement. It is disciplined inquiry, accurate communication, respect for rights, and a practical understanding of how people can participate in public life while remaining accountable to evidence.
